blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights this 1984 paper as a true classic that introduces the 'end-to-end argument'—a design principle guiding the placement of functions in distributed systems. The core idea is that many functions (e.g., encryption, error detection, guaranteed delivery) are best implemented at the application level rather than in lower layers of the system, as only the endpoints can fully ensure correctness. The paper argues that lower-level implementations may be redundant or incomplete, offering only performance enhancements. Colyer notes the paper's influence on layered protocol design and its role as part of a broader set of principles for organizing such systems. He also points to a later critical review that examines why some functions (like congestion control) did migrate into the communications substrate despite the end-to-end argument, due to shared network responsibilities and non-altruistic endpoint behavior.
